sections.html:
• Other names: Acan Lords, Micro Lords
  • Scientific name: Micromussa lordhowensis (previously Acanthastrea sp.)
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (about 40 litres)
  • Keeping: easy to moderate; propagation: easy
  • Lighting: low to moderate; water flow: low to moderate
  • Salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 10 ppm
  • Feeding: photosynthetic
  • Tank placement: bottom
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Toxic: no; invasive: no; aggressiveness: peaceful
  • Colour forms: red, purple, grey, blue, green, brown, pink, orange, etc.

Identifying and buying Acan corals, especially the Acan Lord (Micromussa lordhowensis), can be a bit tricky. It is easier to identify them when the fleshy polyps are fully extended. This helps avoid confusion with Favites and Favia: unlike these corals, the corallite walls of M. lordhowensis are not separate in its skeletal structure; all walls are shared between the individual polyps.

When looking for healthy specimens, choose Acans with a fluffy appearance and bright colours, so you can be sure the coral is not bleached.

Acans can be bought at pet stores and online from retailers. The price varies with rarity, retailer, colour and size. Frags of one or two heads are fairly cheap, but some rare colour variations can cost much more.

Acan corals usually occur in the western Indo-Pacific. Their geographical distribution ranges from the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aqaba and the eastern coast of Africa to the East China Sea, most parts of Australia and the Solomon Islands.

The most common and popular Acan species, Micromussa lordhowensis, takes its name from Lord Howe Island. It is also found around Australia in Flinders Reef, Elizabeth Reef, Middleton Reef, the Dampier Archipelago and the Burrup Peninsula.

Acan corals are commonly found in reef environments, usually at depths of about 0–30 m or more.

In nature, Acan colonies are massive and usually flat, reaching 2–3 metres in diameter. Each coral has a calcium skeleton (corallites) beneath soft fleshy polyps. The corallite is a skeletal cup formed by an individual stony coral polyp, in which the polyp sits and into which it can retract. It can be up to 15 mm in diameter. The septa are thick near the wall of the corallite and have tall fine teeth.

Acan corals come in varying colour combinations and patterns; for instance, M. lordhowensis is often composed of two or more contrasting shades of red, orange, purple, pink, blue or green.

Large tanks starting from 20 gallons (80 L) are recommended, because a larger water volume promotes stability of the water chemistry.

If that is not affordable or practical, a smaller 10-gallon (40 L) tank can be used. As long as water parameters are stable, Acans can be kept in any tank.

Water changes of 20% a month, 10% every two weeks or 5% weekly are needed for tanks housing Acans. A 5% weekly water change is especially important for nano reef tanks: it replenishes many of the needed additives and is cheaper than buying additives for the tank water.

Monitor Acans regularly so that any problem can be discovered and tackled quickly.

Acans appreciate standard saltwater parameters and, despite their hardy nature, will not tolerate drastic changes in water chemistry. High water quality is key to a healthy marine aquarium; many health and algae problems are caused by unstable water quality.

Placement. Placement greatly affects growth. Acans can be placed on the tank bottom, the sand bed or live rock. Keeping an Acan on the tank bottom gives it a ball shape but significantly limits its growth rate. Placing it on the sand bed can be harmful because, with strong water movement, sand can get trapped between the skeleton and tissue and kill the coral. If the coral is fastened to live rock, it grows out uniformly following the shape of the rock, and has great potential to get larger on a large live rock.

Problems.

  • Coral bleaching: the coral's flesh becomes translucent or pale, so the skeleton shows through the tissue. It occurs when the symbiotic zooxanthellae are lost or expelled. Partial bleaching also exists; partial loss of zooxanthellae affects growth and overall health and leaves the coral susceptible to disease. Causes include excessive lighting, high water temperature and extreme changes in salinity.
  • Yellow blotch disease: circular spots of translucent tissue with a yellow tone, or a narrow band of pale tissue at the base of the coral, while other areas stay healthy and keep their natural colour. It is caused by bacteria that cause pale yellow lesions and attack or kill the zooxanthellae, removing the coral's ability to photosynthesise efficiently.
  • White pox: caused by the gram-negative bacterium Serratia marcescens. The coral shows white spots on its surface, which increase in number and size as the bacteria spread and consume the coral's tissue.

• Temperature: 23–26°C for healthy growth and development.
  • pH: 8.1–8.4. It can easily be raised using a buffer.
  • Hardness: KH 8–12 dKH (3–5 meq/l). A low KH can easily be corrected by adding Seachem Reef Carbonate or Reef Builder.
  • Salinity: 1.023–1.025 (total dissolved salts measured as specific gravity).
  • Phosphate: 0.02–0.05 ppm
  • Nitrate: <10 ppm
  • Calcium: 380–450 ppm. Calcium is a building block for corals and vital for longevity; it can be maintained with calcium supplements.
  • Magnesium: 1200–1350 ppm. Magnesium is important for coral growth and for maintaining water pH.
  • Strontium: 8–10 ppm

Acan corals are quite sensitive to phosphate. When levels get too high (0.1 and more), they often shrivel up. In this case, do a water change and stop feeding for a week; they should open up again gradually.

Lighting: Acans do best under low to moderate lighting (20–50 PAR), heavily influenced by the blue spectrum in the 20,000 Kelvin range, which brings out their colours. Avoid strong lighting: depending on the species, it may prevent the polyps from opening fully, cause loss of colouration or even bleach them. Lighting also has a major impact on colour; for example, high light can cause a loss of blue pigments and a deepening of red pigments. The colour of Acans in the store may differ from that in your tank.

Flow: Water flow should be low to moderate, preferably closer to the lower side. Avoid dead spots in the tank. High flow can prevent the corals from opening and make them harder to feed. Enough indirect water movement is needed so they can filter-feed, remove waste products and avoid debris collecting on them. This is best achieved with a wavemaker or alternating powerheads that create laminar flow in the tank. Moderation is key.

Like other animals in the class Anthozoa, Acan corals receive a large portion of their nutrition through photosynthesis from their symbiotic relationship with zooxanthellae algae. In a well-established reef aquarium, Acans can also feed from the water column by consuming phytoplankton and zooplankton suspended in the tank water.

Regular feeding should still be a priority: every 2 or 3 days. Acans are more active at night and extend their tentacles to collect food, but can be fed at any time of day. They accept:

  • copepods
  • shrimp and other meaty foods
  • frozen mysis
  • marine pellets
  • LPS coral pellets and Reef Roids

Corals newly introduced to the tank may not accept food for a while; this is normal, and they begin feeding only once fully acclimated.

Target feeding is advisable to make sure Acans are well fed: use a turkey baster or pipette to direct the food onto their heads, and turn off the pumps for easier feeding. Tip: spray the coral with a trace amount of food to trigger the feeding response after a few minutes; once they sense the food they open their feeding tentacles.

Polyps of the genus Micromussa are generally peaceful towards other corals, but they extend tentacles to feed and can damage other corals, so they should be properly spaced or kept away from other corals. These corals extend their stomachs at night to attack nearby corals.

Acans grow by producing new heads and eventually form a dome shape when fully grown. They can grow so rapidly that they sprout a new head every 7–14 days once feeding needs are met and optimal water parameters are maintained.

Acan corals are generally considered reef safe. There are reports that Camel shrimp and Peppermint shrimp attack these corals. However, people often get the Atlantic Peppermint shrimp (Lysmata boggessi) instead of Lysmata wurdemanni (the Gulf and Caribbean Peppermint shrimp), and Lysmata boggessi is not reef safe.

Large polyp stony corals, including Acans, are hermaphrodites: they possess male and female gametes in the same organism, and can reproduce both sexually and asexually.

Acans are broadcast spawners. In the wild they release eggs and sperm at the same time, producing a fertilised egg that develops into a free-swimming planula larva. After a while the larva settles onto the substrate and eventually metamorphoses into a tiny polyp that begins to excrete calcium carbonate and develops into a coral. Planula larvae are extremely vulnerable to predation, so very few survive.

In captivity, Acans reproduce by dropping tissue when stressed, in an attempt to propagate. They can also be propagated by fragmenting or cutting. The process is simple but requires caution:

  • Make sure your hands are clean or wear gloves.
  • Take out each polyp and cut down the centre of the polyp through the mouth, into halves or quarters. Cutting can be done with a sharp scalpel, blades, bone cutters, a diamond band saw or a Dremel. This is the most difficult part, as Acans are very hard to break cleanly; be careful not to shatter the skeleton.
  • Try to cut around all the 'eyes' of the coral.
  • Afterwards, treat the new frags with an iodine solution (for example, Lugol's solution) to prevent disease, then attach them to live rock before returning them to the tank.
  • Glue the piece to a frag plug. Tip: soak the frag plug in water for a couple of minutes to release air bubbles from the ceramic.

Things you might need depending on the method: hammer and chisel, scissors, cyanoacrylate glue, containers, scalpel or razor blade, plug pebbles or coral frag disks.

Acans grow quite fast; new heads often form only a few weeks after cutting a new frag. If there is no space left, growth slows and they grow by excreting more skeleton and mounding into a larger shape.

There is confusion about the origin and taxonomy of Acan corals. Until a few years ago they were classified in the genus Acanthastrea, which included 8 species. A new study concluded that lordhowensis is much more closely related to other corals of the genus Micromussa than to Acanthastrea, so it was reclassified as Micromussa lordhowensis. Hobbyists are used to the old name, so it will still appear here and there for years to come.

  • Kingdom: Animalia
  • Phylum: Cnidaria
  • Class: Anthozoa (sea anemones, stony corals and soft corals)
  • Order: Scleractinia (stony or hard corals)
  • Family: Lobophylliidae (a family of large polyp stony corals, created in 2009 after a revision of the families Faviidae, Merulinidae, Mussidae and Pectiniidae)
  • Genus: Acanthastrea and Micromussa
